channel.title: DNA Computing Audio Course
channel.description: A personal audio course on computing, analog and digital machines, how AI models are built, and molecular computing. Lessons are numbered in listening order.
channel.itunes:author: DNA Computing Audio Course

item.title: 0.1 The map
item.description: What the course builds and in what order, and the three questions to ask of any computer: what carries the signal, how it is kept clean, and what limits its size.

item.title: 1.1 Bits, gates and the digital abstraction
item.description: What a bit is physically, why a handful of gates is enough to build anything, and the five things a physical system needs before it can be a logic family.

item.title: 1.5 What can be computed, and at what cost
item.description: Turing machines, universality, and why Adleman's experiment could not scale: what massive parallelism buys and what it never will.

item.title: 2.2 The precision bill
item.description: Why each extra bit costs an analog system four times the energy and a digital system one more wire, where the crossover sits, and where the noise in a tube of DNA really comes from.

item.title: 2.4 The analog comeback: why AI reopened the question
item.description: How a grid of resistors multiplies a matrix in one step, what goes wrong when you build it, and what the same structure looks like in chemistry.

item.title: 2.5 Mortal computation: machines that learn in their own physics
item.description: Hinton's argument for hardware whose knowledge cannot be copied, the training methods it needs, and the odd position DNA holds, with a copyable part and a mortal part.

item.title: 2.7 What a bit costs: the thermodynamics of computation
item.description: Landauer's limit, Bennett's reversible computers, the trade between speed, accuracy and energy, and an honest energy account for a DNA gate.

item.title: 2.10 A scorecard for any computing substrate
item.description: Thirteen questions that size up any computer, applied to silicon, the brain, analog chips, a well-mixed DNA circuit and DNA storage.

item.title: 3.4 Backpropagation out loud
item.description: How a network assigns blame to millions of weights in one backward sweep, and the four things that sweep demands of the hardware.

item.title: 3.14 The compute behind AI
item.description: Counting the arithmetic in a training run, what a GPU provides, why memory traffic is the bottleneck, and the workload profile any new hardware has to meet.

item.title: 3.17 Learning without backpropagation
item.description: The menu of learning rules a physical system could run on itself, from Hebbian rules to evolution, and which have been tried in chemistry.

item.title: 4.2 BINND dissected: a design review
item.description: The paper taken apart decision by decision: framing, data, encoding, architecture, training, evaluation and limits, with the questions to ask of any model like it.

item.title: 5.6 Digital circuits in a test tube, and the scaling wall
item.description: How seesaw gates restore signals, what the square-root circuit proved, and the six reasons well-mixed circuits stop growing.

item.title: 5.8 DNA neural networks I: how a tube computes a weighted sum
item.description: Weights as concentrations, sums for free, thresholds and winner-take-all, and what kind of classifier the 2018 network really is.

item.title: 5.10 DNA neural networks II: analog accuracy, reuse and learning in the tube
item.description: The three advances of 2025, what each really showed, and how far learning in chemistry still is from training.

item.title: 5.15 Beyond the well-mixed tube: enzymes, surfaces, compartments and cells
item.description: Why the stirred tube is the least scalable architecture, and what enzymes, tethering, droplets and living cells each buy.

item.title: 5.20 DNA storage as a computer's memory
item.description: Writing, reading and random access, the NC State line of work, and the three ways people have computed on stored data.

item.title: 6.1 Sizing the problem
item.description: What an AI workload costs in operations, memory, precision and sequential steps, and what chemistry offers in each of those currencies.

item.title: 6.2 The design space: seven routes to molecular AI
item.description: Seven architectures, each scored on what has been shown, what binds it, and where a tenfold gain could come from.

item.title: 6.4 The interface and the clock
item.description: The cost and delay of writing and reading molecules, and how to design computations around a cycle time of minutes.

item.title: 6.5 Open problems, and how to choose yours
item.description: Ten open problems, what a result on each would look like, and a way of choosing among them that uses what a chemical engineer is good at.
